title: Houthi blitz leaves Saudi Arabia exposed, Iran emboldened
summary: The lack of international military support for Saudi Arabia, particularly from the US, has emboldened Iran and its allies, complicating the geopolitical landscape in the region

items: The Houthi capture of strategic territory near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait represents a significant setback for Saudi Arabia, revealing intelligence failures and the collapse of Yemeni allies.
The Houthis have amassed a large fighting force and successfully taken advanced weaponry from retreating Saudi-backed forces, which could enhance their military capabilities and leverage.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

ANKARA, Turkey – The Houthi capture of ground overlooking the Bab el-Mandeb Strait deals Saudi Arabia its gravest setback in Yemen in years, exposing intelligence failures, the collapse of Yemeni allies and the limits of US protection.

A Houthi advance this week along the Red Sea coast and the capture of islands at the mouth of the strait, a vital artery for global oil supplies, also leaves the kingdom scrambling for backing as Iran and its allies expand their reach.

Senior Western, regional and Yemeni officials and sources say the Houthi breakthrough reflects various factors: deep divisions among anti-Houthi Yemeni factions, an untested Saudi-led command structure that replaces Emirati oversight, limited Saudi air support and an underestimation of Houthi preparations.

blocks.caption: Saudis pound Yemen as Houthis solidify gains in new theater of Middle East war

blocks.text: The diplomat says the Houthis have quietly assembled about 100,000 fighters, vastly outnumbering forces on the opposing side, adding: “Everyone, including the Saudis, missed this build-up and miscalculated the Houthis’ intentions.”

Neil Quilliam, a fellow at London’s Chatham House think tank, describes the offensive as a glaring intelligence failure, saying: “They just weren’t picking up the signal. They just weren’t seeing the signs.”
Yemeni political analyst Farea Al-Muslimi adds: “The Saudis were caught off guard in Yemen.”
The collapse of Saudi-backed forces hands the Houthis another prize beyond territory — a sizeable cache of advanced US- and Saudi-supplied weaponry abandoned during the retreat.

The haul, according to regional sources, is likely to bolster the group’s military capabilities, provide valuable intelligence on adversaries’ equipment and further reinforce perceptions of a humiliating Saudi defeat.
“The Yemeni government forces were like a house of cards. They didn’t resist. Completely. Completely,” says Abdulkhaleq Abdallah, a political analyst in the United Arab Emirates.

The setback also exposes how limited international support for a counteroffensive may be. Two Western officials say neither the United States nor European countries are prepared to offer direct military backing, and that Washington and its allies have not even joined a Saudi-led maritime defense coalition announced in July.
Saudi officials do not respond to a request to comment.

With Iran-backed fighters now holding territory that can threaten Saudi oil exports and Red Sea shipping, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman (MbS) goes to Cairo to discuss military cooperation between the two countries as Saudi Arabia seeks to contain the fallout after Washington declines to directly intervene militarily.

Two regional sources familiar with the meeting in Egypt say Riyadh wants Egypt to help play a role in Red Sea operations. One regional source says MbS asks President Abdel Fattah ​al-Sisi for military support on Yemen given the close ties between the two countries. There is no immediate word on whether Cairo agrees.

A Saudi source says the meeting is scheduled long before the US-Israeli war against Iran begins in February and “while it obviously covered the latest developments, it had the full agenda of bilateral issues to discuss.”
Egypt’s Foreign Ministry does not immediately respond to a request for comment when asked whether MbS has discussed Egyptian military support.
The Houthis also appear to be using their gains to press for broader political concessions.

Former US negotiator Dennis Ross says the group wants Riyadh to lift restrictions on Hodeidah port and Sanaa airport, provide compensation for the war and scale back support for Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
“I don’t think the Saudis can easily give in to the kinds of demands that they’re making,” Ross says.

A Gulf official says Saudi Arabia now faces a narrowing set of choices. Allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains risks turning tactical victories into lasting strategic leverage, while a larger military response could prompt attacks deeper inside the kingdom.
“If you don’t inflict enough pain on the Houthis, you become hostage to them,” the official says.

Control of territory around Bab el-Mandeb — which lies between Yemen on the Arabian Peninsula and Djibouti and Eritrea on the African coast — could deepen the Houthis’ regional reach, putting the Horn of Africa within easier reach of their logistical and smuggling networks.

MbS’s foreign policy strategy, built on trying to stabilize the region via a détente with Iran, has unraveled since the start of the war as his economic transformation agenda comes under mounting strain, increasing pressure on the kingdom’s de facto ruler.
Combined with Iran’s leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, another vital route for global energy supplies, the foothold gives Tehran and its allies influence over two critical maritime choke points.

The absence of Western military assistance in Yemen, and the absence of these powers from a newly formed defense coalition, exposes the limits of its ability to rally support at a moment of acute vulnerability.
Riyadh appears increasingly to have been outmaneuvered by its adversaries and left wanting by its allies.

The Houthi offensive reveals a blind spot in Saudi and US strategy: while Washington and its allies focus on containing Iran directly, Tehran widens the battlefield by opening fronts from Iraq to the Red Sea, using energy assets, shipping routes and proxies as instruments of pressure.

blocks.caption: US officials met Iran-backed Houthis in Oman over the weekend, sources say

blocks.text: The larger significance of the Houthi breakthrough lies not only in the blow to Saudi Arabia but in the momentum it restores to Iran’s influence across the region, after major setbacks to its allies in Gaza, Syria and Lebanon.
For Iran it’s a “win-win-win,” says Farea Al-Muslimi.

Some political analysts say the more consequential blow is not the battlefield reversal but Washington’s reluctance to come to its ally’s aid. That signal, they say, has emboldened adversaries, weakened Riyadh’s leverage and reinforced doubts over the reliability of US security guarantees.
Al-Muslimi describes Washington’s refusal to help defend Saudi territory as “the biggest dismissing of the Saudi-American arrangement” in decades.
“The Americans are saying No,” he says. “That kind of understanding in the relationship between Riyadh and Washington has never been tested more than now.”

Yemen’s long record of defeating foreign powers – from Egypt in the 1960s to the Soviets and, more recently, the US and Saudi Arabia – helps explain why Riyadh’s search for partners may yield only limited results.

Few regional powers appear eager to be drawn deeper into a conflict that has repeatedly frustrated attempts at outside intervention and acquired a reputation as a graveyard for foreign military ambitions.
“Yemen is the Vietnam and Afghanistan of every power dragged into it,” Muslimi says, referring to conflicts in which foreign powers are humbled.
“The Saudis failed in Yemen, the Americans failed in Yemen,” he says, adding in reference to Egypt’s costly intervention in Yemen in the 1960s: “The Egyptians failed in Yemen.” – Rappler.com
